system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2143-09-04 16:15:00 to 2143-09-10 17:16:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a morbidly obese male with HLA-B27 positive ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, and anxiety, was admitted for acute-on-chronic bilateral sacroiliac joint pain, worse on the left. He reported poor rehabilitation experience after a prior admission and worsening pain at home. Labs showed elevated inflammatory markers without signs of infection. Pain was managed with a return to Dilaudid, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and cyclobenzaprine. Prednisone 20 mg daily was started as a bridge to biologic therapy. Rheumatology recommended outpatient initiation of anti-TNF inhibitors pending infectious disease clearance and Quantiferon Gold testing. The patient improved clinically, was discharged home with home health services, and given a plan for follow-up and medication tapering.
problems: Ankylosing spondylitis sacral and sacrococcygeal region

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  SACRO-ILIAC JTS (AXIAL AND BILAT OBLS)

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with AS about to start TNF  // eval sacro-iliac
joints       eval sacro-iliac joints

TECHNIQUE:  3 radiographs of the sacroiliac joints were obtained

COMPARISON:  CT examination dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

The sacroiliac joints appear NARROWED bilaterally with associated sclerosis
at.  This is unchanged from prior CT examination of ___ and
consistent with ankylosing spondylitis.  There are no Frank erosions.  The
pubic symphysis is unremarkable.

Stool and gas project over the sacrum.

IMPRESSION: 

Known sacroiliitis unchanged from prior CT of ___.  No definite
evidence for infection

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with AS about to start TNF r/o pna  // r/o pna

TECHNIQUE:  Chest PA and lateral

COMPARISON:  ___

FINDINGS: 

No focal consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax identified. 
Unchanged atelectasis/scarring in the right lower lobe.

The size of the cardiac silhouette is mildly enlarged but unchanged.

IMPRESSION: 

No radiographic evidence of acute cardiopulmonary disease.

EXAMINATION:  CT-guided bilateral injections.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with HLA + ankylosing spondylitis presenting with
acute on chronic hip and bilateral SI joint pain. Please perform steroid
injection in b/l sacroiliac joints. Please ___ for any clarification.  //
Long acting steroid injection in SI joints for acute pain exacerbation.
?Inflammation in bilateral SI joints

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___, (radiology fellow) and Dr. ___, radiology
attending, who was present for key points and supervised the procedure.

MEDICATION:  None.

COMPARISON:  Bilateral sacroiliac joint radiographs attempted ___.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:  Following discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, informed written patient consent was obtained. 
The patient was brought to the CT suite and placed prone on the table. An
initial limited noncontrast CT was performed to mark the sites, please see
below for details.

A preprocedure time-out was performed using 3 patient identifiers. The skin
was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Right sacroiliac joint:  Approximately 2cc of 1% lidocaine was infiltrated
into the skin and subcutaneous tissues for local anesthesia. Using
intermittent CT fluoroscopic guidance, a 19 gauge 17 cm needle was advanced
into the right sacroiliac joint.  Upon confirmation of needle position, a 2 cc
solution of 0.25% bupivacaine and 40 mg Kenalog was injected.  The needle was
removed and manual compression was applied achieve hemostasis.

Left sacroiliac joint: Approximately 2cc of 1% lidocaine was infiltrated into
the skin and subcutaneous tissues for local anesthesia. Using intermittent CT
fluoroscopic guidance, a new 19 gauge 17 cm needle was advanced into the right
sacroiliac joint. Upon confirmation of needle position, a 2 cc solution of
0.25% bupivacaine and 40 mg Kenalog was injected.   The needle was removed and
manual compression was applied achieve hemostasis.

 There were no immediate post-procedure complications and the patient left the
department in stable condition.

The patient reported no change in pain symptoms immediately following
injections.

FINDINGS: 

Mild narrowing and subchondral sclerosis of bilateral sacroiliac joints.

IMPRESSION:


1. Mild narrowing and subchondral sclerosis of bilateral sacroiliac joints.
2. Technically successful CT guided bilateral sacroiliac joint steroid
injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of worsening pain in your hips and sacroiliac joints. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. The pain’s been getting worse over the last week and a half. It’s especially bad on the left side. I feel weak, like I might fall. I’ve also had chills and some nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, trouble with bowel or bladder, or numbness in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no numbness or incontinence. I did have a low-grade fever at home—around 99.7—but nothing higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We know you have ankylosing spondylitis, and you were recently on prednisone. Your rheumatologist increased it to 40 mg, but it didn’t help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I called them and they said I should get a methylprednisolone infusion, but I never got it. The pain just got too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll manage your pain here with IV Dilaudid for now. We’ve also ordered blood tests and imaging to check for infection or worsening inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m worried it might be an infection. I’ve had infections before when I was on those TNF drugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of that. That’s why we’re being careful. We’ve already checked your blood cultures and urine. So far, no signs of serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I still don’t know if I want to restart those biologics. They helped with pain, but the infections were scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But given how many times you’ve been admitted for pain, restarting a TNF inhibitor like Symponi might be worth considering—with proper screening first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess. I just need this pain under control first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve scheduled a CT scan of your sacroiliac joints to see if there’s any new damage or signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT results are back. There’s no sign of infection. The joint changes are consistent with your known ankylosing spondylitis and haven’t changed much from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just a flare-up then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your CRP is elevated but lower than last time, which suggests inflammation, but not necessarily active infection. Rheumatology recommends steroid injections into the joints instead of more oral steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Injections? Will that help more than the pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For localized pain like yours, yes. It delivers anti-inflammatory medicine directly to the joint. We’ll schedule it early this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it. What about my blood pressure? It’s been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your BP has been in the 150s. It’s likely due to pain and the steroids you’re on. We’re increasing your lisinopril from 10 to 20 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my breathing? Sometimes I feel tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid. We’ll keep your asthma meds—albuterol, ipratropium, and fluticasone—to help with any tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no growth. The urine culture showed mixed bacteria, but that’s likely contamination, not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. We’ll continue to monitor, but no signs of systemic infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When will I get the injections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for tomorrow morning. Interventional Radiology will do it under CT guidance to make sure it’s precise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder—your injection is at 10 a.m. today. You’ll be awake, but we’ll use local anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel some pressure, but the area will be numbed. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is complete. They injected steroid into both sacroiliac joints. It was technically successful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much. How long before it starts working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can take a few days. We’ll keep managing your pain with oral Dilaudid and acetaminophen in the meantime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your pain is improving. You’re using less pain medication, and you’re moving better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it does feel a bit better. Not gone, but better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The steroid injections often take 3–5 days to peak. We’re also confirming your TB test came back negative—no sign of tuberculosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can start the TNF drug now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your rheumatologist wants to start Symponi. You’ll follow up with them next week. Once you start, we’ll begin tapering your prednisone by 10 mg per week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I guess it’s worth a try. I can’t keep coming back to the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also start Bactrim prophylaxis to reduce infection risk, especially since you’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today look stable. White count is coming down. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue prednisone 40 mg daily until you see your rheumatologist. Then start tapering. We’re also sending you home with Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, acetaminophen, and cyclobenzaprine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, lisinopril 20 mg daily. Please follow up with your PCP to check your blood pressure and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment scheduled. They’ll help coordinate long-term pain management alongside your rheumatologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll need someone to help at home, and you should use your walker for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: follow up with rheumatology to start your TNF inhibitor, and with infectious disease to monitor for any risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I do. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming your discharge instructions: continue prednisone 40 mg daily, taper only after starting Symponi. Use Dilaudid as needed, but not more than every four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the Bactrim?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start that as prescribed by your rheumatologist to prevent infections while on the biologic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call them right after I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your edema has increased slightly. Keep your legs elevated and monitor for worsening swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not painful, just puffy. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It could be from steroids or immobility. But call if it gets worse or you have shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. You’re cleared to go home with home services for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your partner sign the discharge forms. Remember your follow-up appointments: rheumatology, PCP, and pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got them written down. I won’t miss them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. Keep up the follow-up, and we hope this flare stays under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really appreciate all the help. I’m hopeful this new treatment will work.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a morbidly obese male with HLA-B27 positive ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, and anxiety, was admitted for acute-on-chronic bilateral sacroiliac and hip joint pain. He had recently increased his prednisone to 40 mg without relief and missed a planned methylprednisolone infusion. Admission labs showed mild inflammation with normal blood cultures and a contaminated urine culture. Imaging confirmed stable sacroiliitis without infection. He received CT-guided bilateral sacroiliac joint steroid injections, after which his pain improved and he was weaned from IV to oral pain medication. His lisinopril was increased for hypertension, and asthma and anxiety were managed with home medications. The rheumatology plan includes starting a TNF-alpha inhibitor (Symponi) with infectious disease screening completed, including a negative Quantiferon test. He will taper prednisone after initiating biologic therapy and begin Bactrim prophylaxis. He was discharged home with follow-up arranged in rheumatology, pain management, and primary care.
